description: How the lifting of the RAC monopoly opened up British slave trading and reshaped Atlantic commerce.
content_html:
The Royal African Company

The Royal African Company (RAC) was chartered in 1672 under the patronage of the Duke of York (later James II). It held a royal monopoly on English trade with West Africa, including the trade in enslaved Africans. Between 1672 and 1713 the RAC transported an estimated 100,000 enslaved Africans to the Caribbean and North American colonies. Prominent investors included Edward Colston, the Bristol merchant whose involvement in the RAC made his fortune and later became the subject of public debate about how slave traders should be memorialised.

In 1698, Parliament passed the Ten Per Cent Act, breaking the RAC’s monopoly. Any English merchant could now trade in enslaved Africans by paying a 10% duty on goods exported to Africa. This “open trade” decision had catastrophic consequences: the number of enslaved Africans transported by British ships increased dramatically. Between 1700 and 1730, British ships transported an estimated 470,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic — by far the largest such trade of any nation.

Key Fact

The Royal African Company (1672) held the monopoly on English enslaved-person trading until 1698. The Ten Per Cent Act broke the monopoly. British ships then transported an estimated 470,000 enslaved Africans between 1700 and 1730 — around three times the RAC’s total in the previous thirty years.

The Treaty of Utrecht and the Asiento

The Treaty of Utrecht (1713) ended the War of the Spanish Succession and awarded Britain the Asiento — the exclusive contract to supply enslaved Africans to the Spanish American colonies for 30 years. The Asiento was contracted to the South Sea Company, a newly formed joint-stock company. It was enormously prestigious and profitable in theory; in practice the trade proved difficult. The Asiento demonstrates that the slave trade was embedded at the highest levels of British diplomacy and state finance — it was not a peripheral activity but a central prize of international warfare.

The South Sea Bubble was one of the first recorded stock-market crashes. The South Sea Company had taken on part of the national debt in 1711, issuing shares in exchange. Speculation drove the share price from £100 to over £1,000 by mid-1720. When the bubble burst, thousands of investors were ruined. Robert Walpole, who had warned against the speculation, became First Lord of the Treasury in the aftermath and managed the financial rescue — cementing his political dominance for the next two decades. The crisis exposed the dangers of unregulated financial speculation tied to the slave trade.

The Middle Passage and Human Cost

The Middle Passage was the sea crossing from West Africa to the Americas. Enslaved Africans were packed into ships in conditions of extreme overcrowding. Mortality rates on British slave ships in this period ranged from roughly 10% to 25% per voyage, though conditions varied. Disease (particularly dysentery, smallpox and scurvy), dehydration, and deliberate violence killed enormous numbers. Those who survived faced chattel slavery in the Caribbean sugar plantations or American tobacco and rice plantations — conditions of permanent, heritable enslavement with no legal protections.

Key Fact

Key dates: 1672 — RAC chartered; 1698 — monopoly broken (Ten Per Cent Act); 1713 — Treaty of Utrecht, Britain wins the Asiento; 1720 — South Sea Bubble. These events form the arc of Britain’s rise to dominance of the Atlantic slave trade.

The economic importance of the Caribbean colonies to Britain was immense. Sugar from Barbados, Jamaica and other islands generated profits that flowed back to Britain, enriching merchants in Bristol, Liverpool and London. By the early eighteenth century, sugar had become a staple food rather than a luxury. The entire plantation economy rested on the labour of enslaved Africans — the colonies were economically unviable without them. Bristol and Liverpool built civic infrastructure — churches, guildhalls, libraries — partly funded by slave trade profits. The interdependence of British domestic prosperity and colonial slave labour was not accidental or incidental: it was structural.

Enslaved Africans: Experience and Resistance

The experience of enslaved Africans was one of total dispossession. Those who survived the Middle Passage arrived in a world where they had no legal personhood — they were property. On Caribbean sugar plantations, work was brutally demanding: the cutting season ran for most of the year, and conditions of overwork and disease meant that life expectancy was short. Plantation owners relied on continuous importation of newly enslaved people to replace those who died. This demographic reality underlines the human scale of the Atlantic slave trade: it was not a one-time event but a continuous system of violence and death.

Enslaved Africans were not passive victims. Resistance took multiple forms: individual acts of sabotage, slowing work pace, preserving African cultural practices, and larger-scale rebellions. In Barbados, a major plot was uncovered in 1692. In Jamaica, Maroon communities of formerly enslaved people who had escaped into the mountains maintained their freedom and eventually forced the colonial authorities into treaties. The existence of this resistance matters for historical understanding: it shows that enslaved people never accepted the moral legitimacy of their enslavement, even when they could not escape it.
exam_tip_html: When writing about the slave trade, examiners expect you to use accurate terminology: “enslaved African” or “enslaved person,” not “slave” as a noun, which removes agency and historical specificity. For significance questions, you need to show both the economic and the human dimensions — answering only “how much money was made” without discussing the human cost of the Middle Passage will be marked down at higher levels. Know the key dates: 1672 (RAC), 1698 (monopoly broken), 1713 (Asiento), 1720 (South Sea Bubble).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Royal African Company (1672) held the monopoly on English enslaved-person trading until the Ten Per Cent Act (1698) broke it open, causing British slave-trading to expand dramatically: an estimated 470,000 enslaved Africans were transported 1700–1730.
  • The Treaty of Utrecht (1713) awarded Britain the Asiento — exclusive rights to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies — embedding the slave trade at the heart of British foreign policy; the South Sea Company's mismanagement of the contract caused the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720.
  • The Middle Passage killed between 10% and 25% of those transported per voyage; British domestic prosperity, including the sugar economy, was structurally dependent on enslaved labour in the Caribbean and North American colonies.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Royal African Company's role in the slave trade before 1698.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. the RAC held a royal monopoly on English trade in enslaved Africans and transported an estimated 100,000 between 1672 and 1713). Secure: Correct feature with some supporting information. Developing: Vague reference without specific detail. Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) and its impact on Britain's slave trade.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. it ended the War of the Spanish Succession; it awarded Britain the Asiento — the exclusive contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the lifting of the Royal African Company's monopoly in 1698 had such significant consequences for the slave trade.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking the Ten Per Cent Act to open competition, the dramatic rise in enslaved Africans transported (estimated 470,000 in 1700–1730), and the embedding of the slave trade across British commercial society. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one consequence explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the slave economy for Britain's commercial development in the period 1688–c.1730? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument evaluating the slave economy's role (sugar profits, slave ports, Asiento) alongside other commercial developments (EIC, Bank of England), with judgement on the human cost, and counter-argument (e.g. early Quaker opposition, limits of 'significance' without abolition context). Secure: Clear argument across more than one dimension with evidence. Developing: Some argument; may focus on only one aspect. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the South Sea Bubble (1720) showed the dangers of linking state finance to the slave trade.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation showing the South Sea Company's assumption of national debt, speculative inflation of its share price due to expectations of Asiento profits, the crash when reality fell short, and Robert Walpole's subsequent management. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Middle Passage experienced by enslaved Africans.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. overcrowded conditions; mortality rates of roughly 10–25% per voyage from disease and violence) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

glossary_terms.definition: A joint-stock company chartered in 1672 that held a royal monopoly on English trade with West Africa, including the trade in enslaved Africans, until 1698.
Bristol merchant, MP and major investor in the Royal African Company, whose wealth derived significantly from the slave trade; his statue was toppled in Bristol in 2020.
A contract awarded to Britain by the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) granting the right to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies in the Americas for 30 years.
The financial crisis of 1720 caused by the collapse of the South Sea Company's share price after speculative investment inflated a bubble that then burst.
The sea crossing made by ships carrying enslaved Africans from West Africa to the Americas, the second leg of the triangular trade, notorious for appalling conditions and high mortality.
